item.title: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or MSK? Building the Same Event-Driven System Four Ways
item.description:
Open the AWS console and search for “messaging”. You get SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis, MSK, MQ, and a few more that I’m sure someone at AWS is very proud of.

Now try to answer a simple question: my service needs to tell other services that something happened. Which one do I use?

The honest answer from most architecture discussions is “it depends”, which is correct and completely useless. So instead of comparing feature lists, I want to do something different. We’ll take one system, an online store, and let it grow. Every few months a new requirement shows up and breaks the previous design. Each break points to the next service.

item.title: Long-Running Workflows in Plain TypeScript: Getting Started with AWS Lambda Durable Functions
item.description:
Every serverless developer eventually writes a Lambda that does “just one more thing”, and one day it runs for 15 minutes and gets killed halfway through. If you’ve watched a CloudWatch log end abruptly with Task timed out, you know the feeling.

The trouble is that plenty of real business processes don’t finish in minutes. Think of a month-long trial onboarding sequence, or a document pipeline that hands off to a human reviewer. Until recently, the options for workflows like that on AWS weren’t great:

item.title: Event Sourcing with DynamoDB, Lambda and CQRS: A Practical Serverless Guide
item.description:
Take a typical online order. It’s placed, paid for, the delivery address is changed, it ships, and it arrives. Now look at how most systems store that. A single row ends with status = "Delivered", and every earlier version of the row has been overwritten. You can see where the order is now, but you can’t see how it got there.

That’s the built-in limitation of the CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) model: each update replaces the previous state. Event sourcing works the other way round. You never overwrite anything. Each change is appended as a new, immutable event, and the current state is whatever those events add up to. A bank statement is a good comparison: it lists every transaction, not just today’s balance.

item.title: Taming Client Customizations in Multi-Tenant SaaS with a Plugin Architecture
item.description:
Every multi-tenant product I’ve seen goes through the same phase. The first customer signs, then the second, and somewhere around the third you hear the phrase that changes everything: “Could you make it work slightly differently for us?”

None of the individual asks sound scary. One customer wants a small change to how approvals behave. Another wants the dashboard arranged their way. A third would rather get notifications by SMS than by email. Each one looks like a five-minute job with an if (tenant === ...) check, so that’s what goes in.

item.title: Passwordless SMS Login on AWS Cognito Using Custom Auth Challenges and Lambda
item.description:
Passwords cause friction for users and risk for whoever has to store them. In a lot of products, especially mobile ones, it’s nicer to let people type their phone number, receive a short code and be signed in. AWS Cognito doesn’t hide this option. Its custom authentication flow lets you swap the usual password check for whatever proof of identity you choose.

Cognito already handles username/password and social sign-in for you, but real products often need something more specific: one-time codes, magic links, a biometric step, or a verification rule that only your organization uses. Custom auth is the extension point for all of these.

item.title: Fixing the N+1 Query Problem in AWS AppSync with Batch Resolvers
item.description:
A single GraphQL query that returns 100 books with their authors looks harmless. Under the hood, though, it can easily fan out into more than a hundred separate backend calls. That hidden multiplication is the N+1 problem, and if you run GraphQL on AWS AppSync, it is one of the first things that will hurt you as traffic grows.

Before getting into the fix, a quick recap of the moving parts.

item.title: How Big Should a Microservice Be? Using Disintegrators and Integrators to Decide
item.description: “How big should this service be?” is one of the hardest questions in a microservices project, and one of the most expensive to get wrong. Teams adopt microservices for independent scaling, flexibility and faster delivery. Draw the boundaries badly, though, and you end up with the opposite: services nobody can reason about, extra moving parts, and operational overhead that keeps growing. Over time that shows up as rising cloud bills, maintenance that drains the team, and an architecture that looks more like a knot than a design.

item.title: How to Build an AI Agent on Amazon Bedrock: A Hands-On Guide
item.description:
A plain chat model can only talk. It can explain how to book a doctor’s appointment, but it can’t look at a calendar, notice a slot is taken or actually make the booking. That gap between describing a task and doing it is what AI agents fill, and Amazon Bedrock now makes building one a matter of configuration rather than months of plumbing.

In this post I’ll cover what an agent actually is, the building blocks Bedrock gives you, and then build a small agent that manages medical appointments end to end. I’ve also added a list of gotchas I’d want to know about before trying this myself.

item.title: CDK for Terraform (CDKTF) in Practice: Building a Serverless REST API with TypeScript
item.description:
What if you could write your infrastructure in TypeScript, the way you would with the AWS CDK, but have Terraform deploy it instead of CloudFormation? That’s exactly what CDK for Terraform offers, and in this post I’ll show you why the combination is worth a look and then build a small serverless REST API with it from start to finish.

Two approaches to infrastructure as code

There are plenty of IaC tools, but two come up all the time in AWS projects. On AWS, CloudFormation is the native deployment engine, and the AWS CDK sits on top of it. Terraform is the popular alternative that works across clouds. Each has clear strengths and weaknesses.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Explained: Foundation Models, Fine-Tuning, RAG and Agents
item.description:
Adding generative AI to an application used to mean picking a model, finding GPUs to run it on, and keeping that infrastructure alive. Amazon Bedrock removes most of that work. It is a fully managed AWS service that gives you models from several leading AI providers behind one consistent API, so you can skip hosting entirely and start calling models from your code straight away.

Bedrock also goes past plain inference. In this post I’ll walk through the four building blocks I find most useful:

item.title: From Zero to Jenkins on Amazon EKS in Minutes: A Cluster.dev and Helm Walkthrough
item.description:
Most people who love Kubernetes love it for what happens after the cluster exists: self-healing workloads, horizontal scaling, and a consistent way to manage the life cycle of distributed applications. The part nobody enjoys is getting a production-grade cluster up in the first place. That initial setup is where a lot of teams lose days, and sometimes their enthusiasm for Kubernetes altogether.

In this post, I want to show that it doesn’t have to be that way. We’ll go from an empty AWS account to a running Kubernetes cluster with Jenkins installed on it, using two tools that each remove a big chunk of the work: Cluster.dev for the infrastructure and Helm for the application. The goal is a setup that is quick the first time and just as easy to repeat the next time.

item.title: Implementing Feature Flags with AWS AppConfig and Lambda Using CDK
item.description:
What if shipping code and launching a feature didn’t have to happen at the same moment? Feature flags give you that separation. They let you merge and deploy work continuously, keep unfinished features switched off in production, and turn them on whenever the business is ready, without running another deployment.

Because of this, a team can deploy “dark” many times while a feature is still in progress. When the feature is complete, someone flips the flag and users see it. The result is a smoother continuous deployment pipeline, a shorter time-to-market, and less risk that one big release disrupts the whole application.

item.title: Real-Time Messaging on AWS: A Serverless WebSocket API with API Gateway, Lambda and CDK
item.description: Think about the last time you watched a chat thread update by itself, a multiplayer game sync a move, or a dashboard tick over without a refresh. None of that works well if the browser has to keep asking the server “anything new?”. What you want is a channel that stays open so either side can talk whenever it has something to say. WebSockets give you exactly that. On AWS, API Gateway can host that channel for you, so you don’t have to run your own socket servers.

item.title: Keyless AWS Deployments from GitHub Actions: A Practical Guide to OIDC Federation
item.description: If your pipeline deploys to AWS with an access key ID and secret saved in GitHub secrets, you’re carrying around a long-lived credential. Someone has to rotate it, and if it ever leaks, whoever finds it can use it. There’s a cleaner option: let GitHub prove who it is to AWS with OpenID Connect (OIDC), and let AWS give back credentials that expire when the job finishes. In this post I’ll walk through how that trust works and how to set it up on both sides.

item.title: Infrastructure as Real Code: A Practical Introduction to AWS CDK
item.description:
Clicking through a cloud console to set up a queue, a bucket and a few functions is fine once. Doing it again for staging, then production, then a new region, and keeping all of them identical as things change, quickly becomes slow and error-prone. Moving to the cloud and to serverless removes a lot of operational burden, but it doesn’t solve that problem by itself.

From manual setup to Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the usual answer. You describe your infrastructure in files, and a tool turns those files into real resources. The benefits are significant:
